title: 3D MRI visualization in mixed reality for HoloLens
summary: An XR tool that converts breast MRI scans into an interactive 3D hologram, built with hand-tracking and eye-tracking controls for radiologists on Microsoft HoloLens 2.

sections.heading: The problem
body: Radiologists read MRI scans as stacks of flat 2D slices, scrolling through dozens of images to mentally reconstruct a 3D shape. The brief was to skip that reconstruction step entirely: take a breast MRI, build it into an actual 3D volume, and let a radiologist examine it directly in mixed reality.
list: Rotate it, slice through it, zoom in, and annotate findings by voice or text
On a HoloLens 2 headset, with no controller needed
Nobody on the five-person team had used Unity or C# before this project

images.alt: Use-case diagram with Radiologist and Administrator actors: the radiologist chooses a file, visualises images (scroll, rotate, zoom, slice), annotates by text or voice recording and saves progress, while the administrator uploads files for 3D reconstruction, resets annotations and deletes files. An eye-tracking log extends annotation on HoloLens 2 only
images.caption: What the system had to do, and for whom. Scroll, rotate, zoom and slice hang off visualisation; text and voice hang off annotation; the eye-tracking log extends it on HoloLens 2 only.

sections.heading: Approach
body: The pipeline stacks three real engineering problems on top of each other.
list: Medical scans arrive as DICOM, a format Unity has no native support for. We wrote a custom converter in C# that decodes single- and multi-frame DICOM and re-encodes each slice as a texture Unity can use

A stack of 2D slices still isn't a 3D object. A volume creation script assembles them into an actual 3D texture, which then needs a custom GPU shader - extending an open-source base - to render as a solid, semi-transparent structure rather than just a bounding cube, with a hand-built transfer function deciding which densities read as tissue and which as background
All of that has to run inside HoloLens 2's Mixed Reality Toolkit, wired to hand-tracking for manipulating the model and eye-tracking to log where the radiologist actually looks

body: The eye-tracking is the genuine differentiator: gaze data can surface which parts of a scan draw clinical attention, which is not something a conventional viewer records at all.

images.alt: The application's start scene as built in Unity, with a press-to-start prompt for the radiologist and a key combination for administrator file upload
images.caption: The app's start scene, built in Unity - press to start as the radiologist, or a key combination for admin file upload.

sections.heading: My part
body: I worked on the third piece: getting everything to run as one system on the headset. That meant integrating MRTK, wiring hand-interaction - rotate, scale, move - directly to the rendered volume, and connecting the holographic UI so the pipeline behaved as a single tool rather than as separate pieces that happened to compile.
list: Researched the options and picked the team's onboarding path, the Unity Essentials course, since nobody was starting with any Unity or C#
Helped structure how the work was split across the team once everyone had the basics

sections.heading: Result
body: Five people, no prior Unity or C# experience, one working end-to-end pipeline: DICOM upload, through volume rendering, to an interactive hologram on a real HoloLens 2, demonstrated on video.

images.alt: The rendered MRI volume as a hologram, viewed through HoloLens 2 during the demo
images.caption: The volume as a hologram on the headset - the end of the pipeline, and the only part a radiologist would actually see.

sections.heading: What actually cost us time
body: The most instructive failure wasn't technical, it was infrastructure.
list: Git couldn't handle the project at all - Unity's mix of large binary and text files broke standard pushes
Git LFS looked like the fix until we hit its 1GB storage quota
That forced a switch to Unity's own version control mid-project, which allows three simultaneous users on a student licence, for a team of five
The rest of development ran on manually coordinated, ad-hoc syncs to work around a three-seat limit for five people - time that should have gone into features
It is also why there's no public repository here: the project lived on Unity Cloud behind that restricted student licence
